title: Optimaviz
description: A data platform stops talking in dashboards and starts speaking in light.
overview: Optimaviz had built an intelligence layer that could read a business in real time. The problem was that every competitor claimed the same thing. We needed a film that made insight feel like a physical force — sixty seconds a CFO would remember and a founder would share.
challenge:
Enterprise analytics is abstract by nature. Dashboards all look alike, feature lists blur together, and buyers have learned to tune out product demos. With no budget for a traditional shoot and six weeks to launch, we had to create a visual world from scratch — without inventing a single product claim.

The film also had to work silently in a LinkedIn feed, with sound in a boardroom, and as a 15-second cutdown. One idea, three very different attention spans.
approach:
We stopped filming software. Instead, we treated data as a natural phenomenon: rivers of warm light moving through vast, quiet architecture. Nothing on screen was a UI. Everything on screen was a consequence of intelligence at work.

The narrative was built in the edit — a slow build from darkness to clarity, cut to an original ambient score. AI generation gave us locations no budget could reach; traditional editing discipline kept it from becoming a showreel of pretty accidents.

pillars.title: Emotion before explanation
pillars.body: The viewer should feel the value of clarity before they understand a single feature.

pillars.title: One visual metaphor
pillars.body: Data as light. Every shot, transition and sound choice serves that single idea.

pillars.title: Sound-led pacing
pillars.body: The score was composed first; the edit was cut to its breath and swells.

process.body: Two weeks with the product and sales teams, mapping the moment buyers actually lean in.
Light tests, lens references and a strict palette: amber, charcoal, no blue-tech clichés.
Runway, Kling and Veo for environments; Midjourney for boards; practical plates for texture.
Cut in Resolve to an original ambient score, then layered foley and designed transitions.
Filmic contrast, halation, grain and clean-up — reviewed on phone, laptop and cinema display.

beforeAfter.note: The grade was designed to feel like light passing through dust — warm highlights, held shadows, and a fine 35mm grain.

testimonial.quote: Ropona took a product feature we'd struggled to explain for a year and turned it into something people actually felt. The film did more for our pipeline than three quarters of paid media.
testimonial.name: Daniel Okafor

title: TaskGo
description: The city wakes up, and so does the errand.
overview: TaskGo needed to move from 'the app that runs your errands' to a brand people trusted with their morning. The answer was not a discount. It was a feeling: the city as a living thing, and one person moving through it while everyone else sleeps.
challenge:
The category was drowning in price-led creative. Every competitor sold speed and convenience with the same bright, loud grammar. TaskGo had three weeks, a modest production budget, and a limited window with real riders.

We had to shoot fast, stay honest to Lagos, and build a film that worked as a 45-second anthem and as six platform cutdowns.
approach:
One continuous dawn, told in fragments. We followed real riders on their first run of the day, shooting available light with a small crew and a long lens. AI previz helped us plan impossible light; practical plates kept the streets real.

The edit finds the story in small gestures — a helmet click, a gate opening, steam off a flask — and builds to the city fully awake. The grade holds teal shadows and warm streetlight, like the hour before the sun takes over.

pillars.title: Real people, real streets
pillars.body: No actors, no studio. The authenticity is the production value.

pillars.title: One city, one morning
pillars.body: Every scene belongs to the same 42 minutes of dawn light.

pillars.title: Built for the feed
pillars.body: The 45-second cut was written to survive muted, vertical and three seconds of scroll.

process.body: Two dawn ride-alongs with TaskGo riders before a single frame was planned.
AI-generated light studies mapped the route and the exact minute each shot needed.
Small crew, available light, real riders — captured across three neighbourhoods.
Anthem first, then eight platform edits built from the same visual grammar.

beforeAfter.note: The grade leans into pre-sunrise blue and sodium-vapour amber — a palette drawn directly from the streets we shot.

testimonial.quote: She directs like an editor and edits like a director. Every frame had a reason to be there — and the turnaround was faster than our traditional pipeline by weeks.
testimonial.name: Sarah Mitchell

title: WayBackHistory
description: History, remembered the way it felt.
overview: A three-part series for a history publisher with a simple brief: make the past feel present. Not a lecture. Not a slideshow of archival stills. A film that puts the viewer inside a moment they have only ever read about.
challenge:
Archive-led history content has two failure modes: it either feels like a museum audio guide, or it drifts into historical fiction with no rigour. WayBackHistory needed scale too — three episodes in six weeks, with a small editorial team and limited rights budget.

Every reconstruction had to be defensible, visually consistent, and clearly framed as interpretation rather than record.
approach:
We built each episode around a single human moment, then reconstructed only what the archive could support: light, texture, objects, weather, silhouettes. Faces were kept partial or turned away — a deliberate choice that protected accuracy and made the films feel like memory rather than re-enactment.

AI generation handled environments and period detail; traditional documentary editing handled structure, narration, and restraint. The grade is built on parchment, dust and low winter sun.

pillars.title: Rigour over spectacle
pillars.body: Every generated frame traces back to a reference, a source, or a note in the research doc.

pillars.title: Memory, not re-enactment
pillars.body: Partial faces and abstract detail keep the films honest and emotionally open.

pillars.title: A repeatable system
pillars.body: Character, period and grade libraries let a small team ship weekly without drift.

process.body: Source-first research with citations, reference boards and a period-accurate visual bible.
Each episode built as a three-act essay around one decision or turning point.
AI environments, objects and atmospheres generated from archival references, then composited.
Narration-led pacing with designed silence, foley and a restrained original score.
Period QC across episodes, grade consistency, grain and archival texture.

beforeAfter.note: Archive plates were stabilised and graded toward aged paper and window light — never sepia, which reads as costume.

testimonial.quote: The rare creative who understands both the craft and the commercial. We came for a video; we left with a visual language for the whole brand.
testimonial.name: Amara Eze

title: AURA
description: A fragrance campaign built from light, glass and gravity.
overview: A launch film for an AI-native fragrance brand that existed before its first physical bottle. With no product to shoot, the film had to make the object feel more real than a sample ever could — and build a world the brand could own.
challenge:
Luxury fragrance advertising is a craft of surfaces: glass, liquid, skin, light. With no physical product, every reflection and refraction had to be invented without the frame drifting into uncanny CGI.

The film also needed to launch across paid social, retail screens and a brand site — each with different aspect ratios and sound conditions.
approach:
We designed the bottle in 3D first, then used generative tools for the fluid behaviour and atmospheric elements. The camera language is deliberately macro and slow: the product is treated like a landscape, not a pack shot.

Sound design carries the luxury — glass tones, low sub, a breath of room — so the film still feels expensive on mute. Gold is used as a material, never a filter.

pillars.title: Design the object first
pillars.body: A solid 3D base kept the bottle consistent through every generated shot.

pillars.title: Macro as landscape
pillars.body: Slow moves and shallow focus make small surfaces feel monumental.

pillars.title: Luxury in the mix
pillars.body: Sound design does as much brand work as the image.

process.body: Bottle form, glass thickness and label geometry modelled before generation.
Gold, amber and black references; tests for caustics, refraction and fluid tension.
Liquid simulations, atmospheric passes and clean-up composited around the hero object.
One 30-second anthem plus vertical, square and silent-first edits.

beforeAfter.note: The finish leans on specular restraint: bright where the glass catches light, never golden everywhere.

title: MONOLITH
description: A short film about the things we build and then forget to understand.
overview: A self-initiated seven-minute short made to test a question: can a fully AI-produced film hold a silence? Monolith follows two surveyors crossing a desert to measure an object that should not exist.
challenge:
Short films made with generative tools often rely on novelty. I wanted the opposite: long takes, minimal dialogue, and a visual grammar that would feel at home in a cinema. The production had to maintain a single sun direction, one palette, and a consistent landscape across hundreds of generations.

With no crew and no location budget, every frame also had to be built in a way that could be revised without starting over.
approach:
The film was designed like a live-action production: a proper screenplay, a shot list, a floor plan, and a continuity bible. I built a desert library first — dunes, rock, haze, horizon — then treated the monolith as a fixed set piece with consistent scale and shadow.

Silence is the main character. The sound design strips almost everything away, leaving wind, footsteps, and a low tone that arrives before the object does.

pillars.title: Write for silence
pillars.body: The story is carried by scale, duration and what the characters refuse to say.

pillars.title: One sun, one landscape
pillars.body: A continuity bible locks light direction, palette and geography across every shot.

pillars.title: Cinema grammar
pillars.body: Wide, wider, close. The edit refuses the montage rhythm typical of AI reels.

process.body: A 9-page script and a beat sheet built around three long sequences.
Desert library, monolith scale tests, and a strict shot-by-shot continuity map.
Generative plates, compositing and practical grain passes across six weeks.
Assembly to temp score, then an original ambient composition and final mix.
4K master, DCP-ready delivery, closed captions and stills package.

beforeAfter.note: The grade keeps the sky almost colourless; warmth lives in the sand and the object's edge.

title: ATELIER
description: A fashion film cut to the rhythm of fabric in motion.
outcome: Campaign film for Paris Fashion Week
overview: A 90-second fashion film for a couture capsule shown at Paris Fashion Week. The footage was shot by a separate director; I came in as editor and colourist to find the film inside it.
challenge:
The rushes were beautiful but structurally loose: long runway walks, fabric tests, and a model performance with no clear narrative spine. The film had to feel like a statement, not a lookbook, and it had to sync to a commissioned score that was still being written.

The colour also had to hold a deep crimson without clipping, on everything from a phone to a projection wall.
approach:
I built the edit around the movement of the fabric itself — the cut lands on a fold, a turn, a collapse. Dialogue and voiceover were removed entirely; the model's breath and the room tone became the narrative.

For the grade, I isolated the red into its own texture: rich in shadow, desaturated at the edges, with skin kept warm and natural. The result is less 'fashion video' and more portrait.

pillars.title: Cut on movement
pillars.body: Transitions are motivated by fabric and body, never by a music beat alone.

pillars.title: Remove the explainer
pillars.body: No voiceover. The film trusts the image to carry the idea.

pillars.title: Protect the red
pillars.body: A dedicated grade pipeline keeps crimson rich without losing detail.

process.body: Selects, scene mapping and a paper edit before touching the timeline.
Three-act assembly built around movement and breath, not chronology.
Sound design and temp score used to test pace with the client.
Crimson isolation, skin protection, grain and projection test.

beforeAfter.note: The crimson was pulled back from digital red into a deeper, fabric-like tone; skin was protected throughout.

title: PULSE
description: A performance that falls apart, one frame at a time.
overview: A music film for an independent artist's single 'Dissolve'. The director shot a single continuous performance in smoke and hard light; my job was to make the image disintegrate in sync with the track without losing the human performance at its centre.
challenge:
The brief was conceptually simple and technically delicate: the performer should appear to dissolve into particles as the song builds. Too much effect and the performance disappears; too little and the idea never lands.

We also had a hard deadline tied to the release date and a fixed post budget.
approach:
I treated the effect as an edit problem first. The performance was cut normally, then the disintegration was mapped shot by shot, starting in the shadows and edges and only reaching the face at the final chorus.

Particle passes were generated from the plate itself, so the image always dissolved into its own texture. The grade keeps contrast high and colour almost absent, letting the warm key light do all the emotional work.

pillars.title: Performance first
pillars.body: The effect never obscures the artist's face until the story earns it.

pillars.title: Dissolve into itself
pillars.body: Particles are sampled from the original plate, keeping the image coherent.

pillars.title: Cut to the vocal
pillars.body: The disintegration follows breath and phrasing, not just the beat.

process.body: One performance, multiple angles; cut for vocal phrasing before effects.
A frame-by-frame disintegration plan tied to the arrangement.
Plate-derived particles, edge erosion and light-wrap compositing.
High-contrast finish, grain, and platform masters for release day.

beforeAfter.note: The grade was pushed toward near-monochrome so the warm key light and the particles carry all the colour.

results.label: pick on a leading music platform

title: MERIDIAN
description: A coastline told as a single, unhurried breath.
overview: A destination brand film for a coastal hospitality group. The brief: sell the feeling of arriving, not the amenities. With properties spread across a coastline that would take weeks to shoot, the film needed a visual journey that felt continuous.
challenge:
Travel films default to drone montage: waterfall, sunset, infinity pool. Meridian wanted restraint and a sense of place. There was also no budget for a multi-location shoot, and the film had to work as a 60-second brand piece and a 15-second booking ad.

The locations had to feel like one continuous coastline, even though they were generated and composited from different references.
approach:
We built the film as one drive down the coast: cliffs, water, a room, a table, a swim. Each shot is held long enough to breathe, with transitions hidden in water and rock. AI environments extended real reference plates and created the impossible aerial continuity.

Sound is the travel: wind, distant surf, a single piano note. The grade leans into the last twenty minutes of daylight — deep teal water, warm rock, no oversaturation.

pillars.title: Sell arrival
pillars.body: The film is about the moment the city noise stops, not a list of facilities.

pillars.title: One continuous coast
pillars.body: A visual map hides the joins between locations and generated plates.

pillars.title: Hold the shot
pillars.body: Longer takes and minimal cuts give the viewer room to want to be there.

process.body: A single coastal route mapped from reference photography and property footage.
Licensed aerials and practical footage used as the backbone for extension.
Coastline, water and architectural shots generated to match the route.
60-second anthem, 15-second booking edit, and silent social versions.

beforeAfter.note: Water was graded toward deep teal to contrast the warm rock and keep the coast from looking like a postcard.

title: PathForge
description: An education brand film about the moment before everything changes.
overview: PathForge helps people change careers. Their marketing explained the how; it never captured the why. We made a film about the first step — the quiet, unglamorous decision to begin — and built a campaign around that moment.
challenge:
Education advertising is crowded with outcomes: salaries, certificates, job placements. PathForge wanted to stand for something less transactional: courage. But courage is hard to show without drifting into cliché.

We also had to speak to two audiences at once — career changers and the employers who fund their teams' development — without blurring the message.
approach:
We built the film around small, recognisable moments rather than big declarations: an empty desk at night, a browser tab left open, a hand reaching for a light switch. AI generated intimate interiors and impossible transitions between them, while real voiceover testimonies grounded the piece in truth.

The edit moves at the pace of a held breath. The final frame is not a graduation, but a start.

pillars.title: Show the before
pillars.body: The film lives in the moment of doubt, not the success story.

pillars.title: Real voices
pillars.body: Actual learner testimonies anchor the generated imagery in truth.

pillars.title: One ask
pillars.body: Every frame points to a single action: take the first step.

process.body: Six learner conversations distilled into a single emotional through-line.
A 500-word narrative pared down to 90 seconds and one idea.
Intimate interiors and transitions generated from reference photography.
Voice-led edit, warm grade, and a six-cutdown enrolment campaign.

beforeAfter.note: Warm practical light and deep shadow make the generated rooms feel lived in rather than designed.
